blocks.text: Acts recounts Paul’s encounter more than once, with rhetorical differences among the accounts. Here the narrative emphasizes both his reversal from persecuting Jesus’ followers and his commission as a witness sent to Jews and Gentiles. “Conversion,” “prophetic call,” and “commissioning” are overlapping ways readers have described this event, though their precise relationship remains debated.

Acts’ fuller portrayal of this encounter includes Paul’s temporary blindness, being led by others, fasting, Ananias’s touch, the return of sight, baptism, food, and entry into mission. This keeps dependency and care within the call narrative, without requiring that recovery come before vocation or identifying this event with Paul’s “thorn.”

Questions about Acts’ historical reliability are best considered claim by claim, comparing particular statements with independent evidence rather than treating the entire work as simply reliable or unreliable. Acts is preserved in early papyri and major Greek manuscripts with differing textual profiles; Codex Bezae and related witnesses preserve a notably distinctive form of Acts. Individual readings, like individual historical claims, require case-by-case judgment.
